title: Half a liter an hour
objective: Recognize diabetes insipidus from large volumes of dilute urine and rising sodium, give desmopressin, and watch for hyponatremia once treatment starts

brief.situation: 23:00 in a neuroscience ICU. You are Mr. Brandt's nurse. He is 49, on the evening of a transsphenoidal resection of a pituitary adenoma. His hourly urine has been 350, then 420, then 500 mL, clear as water.
handover: He has had only the ordered maintenance IV fluid since surgery. He keeps asking for water but is drowsy between requests.

Orders: hourly intake and output, urine specific gravity and serum sodium if output exceeds 250 mL/h for two hours, and call neurosurgery. The ordered desmopressin is to be given only on the neurosurgeon's call.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each assessment takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Why is he passing so much urine, and what do you do now and after treatment?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Central DI (AVP deficiency) after transsphenoidal surgery: polyuria of very dilute urine (low specific gravity), rising sodium and a negative balance, with osmotic diuresis ruled out.
parts.modelAnswer: He's making 400 to 500 mL an hour of urine with a specific gravity of 1.002, his sodium is climbing and he's 2 liters down. His glucose is normal. After pituitary surgery that's central diabetes insipidus.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Calls neurosurgery now; gives the ordered desmopressin and replacement fluid; never restricts fluid; then monitors sodium closely for hyponatremia as the urine slows.
parts.modelAnswer: Call neurosurgery now for desmopressin and replacement fluid. Don't restrict fluids, he's losing water. Once it works, check his sodium every couple of hours, because water retention can drop it too low.

noProgress.rationale: Diabetes insipidus with a rising sodium untreated for an hour is harm here.

expertPath.text: Intake and output: 1,270 mL out in 3 hours. Specific gravity 1.002, sodium rising.
Central DI. Call neurosurgery: desmopressin, replacement, sodium plan.
Give the desmopressin, start replacement matched to output.
Sodium every 2 hours for hyponatremia as the urine slows; document.

seizure.headline: Hypernatremic seizure
seizure.body: Large volumes of dilute urine with a rising sodium after pituitary surgery is DI. Replace the water and give desmopressin; never restrict fluid.

treated.headline: Recognized and treated
treated.body: You recognized central DI from the output, specific gravity and sodium, called within minutes, gave desmopressin and replacement, and planned sodium checks for the swing the other way. That is the expert path.

treatedGaps.headline: Treated, with gaps
treatedGaps.body: Check how soon you called, whether the losses were replaced, and whether fluids were restricted.

time_up.headline: Untreated
time_up.body: DI with a rising sodium needs desmopressin and replacement within the hour.

scoring.modelReasoning: After transsphenoidal surgery, 350 to 500 mL an hour of urine with a specific gravity of 1.002, a sodium rising from 143 and a 2-liter negative balance, with a normal glucose, is central diabetes insipidus: too little vasopressin. Call neurosurgery now, give the ordered desmopressin and replacement fluid matched to output, and never restrict fluid in a patient losing free water. Once the desmopressin works, water retention can drive the sodium too low, so check sodium every 2 hours and watch for output falling sharply.

afterQ.ask: While you wait for the repeat sodium: what is the main risk once desmopressin works?
afterQ.explain: Water retention after desmopressin can drop the sodium; monitor electrolytes closely.
